common_name: Manetti Rootstock Rose (Historic Vigorous Budding Understock)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown rootstock liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then bud a desired rose variety onto the young rootstock; Manetti was one of the earliest widely used commercial rose rootstocks, dating to the 1830s.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown rootstock liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then bud a desired rose variety onto the young rootstock. Manetti, believed to be a hybrid of Noisette and China rose ancestry introduced in Italy in the 1830s, was one of the earliest and longest-used commercial rose rootstocks, valued historically for its ease of propagation from hardwood cuttings, compatibility with a wide range of budded varieties, and relatively few thorns, which made handling easier for commercial growers compared to some other understocks. It produces small, semi-double pink flowers of modest ornamental value on its own, and it has been largely superseded by Dr. Huey and Fortuniana in modern commercial rose production but remains of historical interest and is still used by some specialty growers. As with other rootstocks, any suckering growth from below a graft union should be removed promptly to keep the budded variety's energy directed to the desired top growth.

common_name: Old Gay Hill Rose (Found Texas Red China-Type Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Old Gay Hill is a 'found rose' rescued from an old cemetery near Gay Hill, Texas, prized for reliable red bloom and toughness in Gulf South heat.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil. Old Gay Hill is a 'found rose' of China-type character, rescued by rose rustlers from an old cemetery near the community of Gay Hill, Texas, and named for that location since its original commercial identity was lost. It bears clusters of red, semi-double flowers in nearly continuous flushes through the warm season on a vigorous, well-branched shrub well adapted to Gulf South heat and humidity. Like other found roses rescued from long-neglected sites, it is notably tough and disease-resistant, needing no spray program and tolerating drought and poor soil far better than modern hybrid roses. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead or crossing wood.
sources: The Antique Rose Emporium — Found Rose Collection
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Earth-Kind Rose Trials

common_name: Blush Damask Rose (Classic Soft Pink Once-Blooming Damask)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Blush Damask is a classic 18th-century damask rose blooming once in a heavy spring flush.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Blush Damask, documented since the late 1700s, bears fully double, softly quartered flowers in a gentle blush-pink deepening slightly toward the center, with the rich, classic damask fragrance long prized in perfumery. It blooms once in a heavy flush in late spring to early summer on a dense, upright, thorny shrub typical of the damask class. Its soft coloring and strong fragrance have kept it a favorite in heirloom and cottage-style rose gardens for over two centuries. Like other damask roses it tolerates lean soil and general neglect far better than modern hybrid roses, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.
